headline: Ecosystems are webs of connection—every species depends on others to survive
universal_truth: Nothing exists in isolation; everything is connected to something else
fun_facts: Removing one species from an ecosystem can cause a cascade of unexpected changes to dozens of others
Wolves returning to Yellowstone changed the course of rivers by affecting where deer grazed
A single tree can support hundreds of species—insects, birds, fungi, bacteria—all interconnected
discussion_questions: What connections in nature are invisible but essential?
How might a small change in one part of an ecosystem affect the whole?
What are you connected to that you rarely think about?

hook.script: When wolves returned to Yellowstone, the rivers changed course. How? Wolves reduced deer populations. Deer stopped overgrazing riverbanks. Plants grew back. Roots stabilized soil. Rivers stopped eroding. One species changed the landscape. Everything connects.

cliff.script: We see individual animals and plants. But nature is really a web of relationships. How do ecologists understand these invisible connections?
cliff.prompt: How do scientists study ecosystem connections?

options.text: They track how energy and nutrients flow through food webs and observe what happens when species are added or removed
options.response: Yes. Following energy—who eats whom—reveals the web. Removing one strand shows what it was holding up. Connections reveal themselves through change.

options.text: They count populations and study individual species separately
options.response: Population studies help, but understanding connections requires looking at relationships...

fact1.title: Food Webs
fact1.script: Energy flows through ecosystems in food webs—plants capture sunlight, herbivores eat plants, predators eat herbivores. Each level depends on the level below. Remove one level and everything above it collapses.

fact2.title: Keystone Species
fact2.script: Some species have outsized effects—keystone species. Wolves, sea otters, bees: remove them and ecosystems transform dramatically. Not all species are equally important to the web's structure.

fact3.title: Hidden Dependencies
fact3.script: Many connections are invisible. Fungi connect tree roots underground, sharing nutrients across forests. Bacteria in soil make nitrogen available to plants. The most important relationships are often the ones we can't see.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Nothing exists in isolation. Ecosystems teach that everything connects to something else. Understanding these connections—visible and invisible—reveals how the world actually works.

outro.script: That's Day 151—we're past five months! Tomorrow, we'll explore where species belong. Until then, consider your own web of connections—who and what do you depend on?

growTrack.title: Connection Mapping - See Your Web
growTrack.activity: Map your own 'ecosystem'—what do you depend on? Food from farmers, electricity from power plants, ideas from teachers. Draw your web of dependencies. Like ecosystems, you're connected to more than you realize.
